name: Puzzle
subtitle: Centered around information hiding and inference to create solution spaces; the core is learning curves and hint strategies.
demoRuleHint: Rule: Observe information → Perform action → Receive feedback → Infer next step → Achieve goal
problemsSolved: Clearly define objectives and actionable objects, avoiding the question 'What am I supposed to do?'
Use tiered hints to reduce frustration costs, encouraging players to keep trying.
Make trial-and-error feedback verifiable (correct/incorrect/progression), avoiding randomness and misdirection.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the puzzle loop — observe → act → verify feedback → reason the next step — and reproduce one trial and one hint in the demo
Intermediate: write the feedback contract (instant right/wrong/neutral verification) and the graded-hint policy (budget, tiers, trigger timing)
Advanced: design reasoning-chain length ramps and the learning curve, and verify puzzle health with stuck rate, hint usage rate, and time-between-insights
minimalRules: Goal: satisfy conditions (minimum: reach endpoint / trigger mechanism).
Feedback: every step can be verified (correct / incorrect / neutral).
systemLoopHint: Input → Judgment → Feedback → State change → New input

combos.effect: Physics causal chains provide richer solution spaces.
Reconfiguring the state increases replayability, but explainability must be controlled.
Gradually unlock tools and rules, expanding reasoning ability.

advancedWarnings: Lack of verifiable feedback prevents players from assessing progress.
Too strong hints break the sense of achievement; too weak hints lead to abandonment.
When the solution is unique but the path is long, frustration is amplified.
Too many hints weaken the challenge; too few cause players to get lost—balancing information is the core design trade-off.
Excessive randomization can increase replayability but undermines causal chain explainability, making players feel purposeless.
Over-simplifying hints can actually increase curiosity—players will proactively try multiple strategies when lacking clues.
advancedAlgoRefs: Levels: solvability verification, solution search, hint generation
State: state machine / condition graph, used to express causal chains

demoLab.title: Trial-and-Error Verification
demoLab.action: Without reasoning, click "Try (primary)" ten times and watch mistakes and progress diverge
demoLab.observe: Every step returns a right/wrong signal — mistakes climbing while progress stalls means you are guessing. Verifiable feedback is the minimal rule of puzzles: without it, players cannot tell whether they are advancing or regressing

demoLab.title: Hint Cost Experiment
demoLab.action: Get stuck on purpose, click "Hint (secondary)", then continue — watch the hints budget drain
demoLab.observe: Hints lower the cost of being stuck but spend a budget — too strong kills the achievement, too weak causes abandonment. Graded hints essentially convert "quit rate" into "resource spend": players buy back their sense of accomplishment

demoLab.title: Difficulty Curve Contrast
demoLab.action: On easy vs hard, "Advance 1 Step" 10 steps each and compare difficultyScore and mistake growth
demoLab.observe: On hard, difficultyScore is higher and mistakes grow faster — difficulty is not "a better-hidden answer" but "a longer reasoning chain." Learning-curve design controls how fast the chain lengthens, not how deeply the answer is buried

intro.what: Observe the clues, reason it out, and find the one solution — Sokoban, Monument Valley, and escape-room games are built on this.
intro.feel: You stare at the layout in deep thought, try a step, read the feedback, try again; the "aha" moment arrives like a door swinging open — the agony of being stuck and the ecstasy of insight are two sides of one coin.
intro.why: A core specimen of learning-curve design — how to keep players stuck-but-not-quitting is the most important lesson puzzles teach.

concept: Puzzle play is a carefully engineered "duration of confusion": information is deliberately withheld, the reasoning chain is sized to be just barely walkable, and every trial returns verifiable feedback. The hard part is not a clever riddle — it is managing the cost of being stuck: hints that are too strong kill the achievement, too weak cause abandonment, and unverifiable feedback leaves players unsure whether they are advancing or regressing. The joy of insight is farmed precisely by the rhythm of information disclosure.
designNotes: Hints trade abandonment rate for resource spend: graded hints let players "buy back their sense of achievement" — the hint budget turns a stuck moment from a churn point into a decision point.

Difficulty is not hiding deeper — it is chaining longer: a long reasoning chain with per-step verification beats a "well-hidden answer," because the former gives progress while the latter only invites guessing.

Slightly missing clues spark exploration (counterintuitive): when information runs a little scarce, players voluntarily try multiple strategies — but only if every step’s feedback is honest; otherwise scarcity becomes deception.

value.player: Puzzles sell the "aha" moment: information is deliberately withheld and the player completes it with their own reasoning — an achievement that cannot be lucked into, and is precious for exactly that reason. The agony of being stuck and the joy of insight are carefully rationed by the designer into a unique intellectual high.
value.ecosystem: Puzzle is a word-of-mouth long-tail category: costs are controllable, content production IS level design, and a small team with brilliant levels can build a brand (Monument Valley, Baba Is You).
value.transfer: Learn puzzles and you learn the rhythm of information disclosure — what to hide, when to hint, how to let players walk to the answer themselves — a craft that transfers to tutorial design, narrative guidance, and even product onboarding.
